properties.title: Toward Safe Autonomous Robotic Endovascular Interventions using World Models
properties.contribution: Adaptation and preclinical evaluation of a TD-MPC2 navigation controller against model-free SAC.

properties.name: TD-MPC2 multitask navigation agent

This manuscript is a preprint and has been submitted to the IEEE/RSJ
International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026.

Observations com-
prised current and previous device positions, target location,
and previous action.

A computed tomography angiography (CTA) scan of
the aortic arch and the cerebral vessels, and a CTA scan
encompassing the abdominal and thoracic regions, includ-
ing the femoral arteries, descending aorta, and the aor-
tic arch (obtained with UK Research Ethics Committee
24/LO/0057), were processed into surface meshes using 3D
Slicer (v5.10) [10]. The centerlines and radii for all scans
were extracted.

to generate a surface mesh to be loaded into the Simulation
Open Framework Architecture (SOFA, v23.12) [24]. This
was repeated for 15 aortic arch and cerebral vessel CTAs (15
to capture anatomy heterogeneity associated with challenging
real-world navigation across diverse age/ethnicity/sex), with
the same CTA of the abdominal and thoracic regions (same
CTA as anatomy is homogeneous and real-world navigation
is not challenging) being scaled to fit each one. Type-I aortic
arches were found in 87% (13/15) of vasculatures, while the
remaining were Type-II [25]. Five out of the 15 vasculatures
were used as a hold out dataset forin silicoevaluation
(comprising 80% Type-I and 20% Type-II aortic arches).
C. In silico testbed & data collection
Thein silicoenvironment utilized the stEVE frame-
work [17]. A0.0441”multipurpose (MP) catheter (Terumo,
Tokyo, Japan and0.035”guidewire (Terumo, Tokyo, Japan)
were used for allin siliconavigation tasks. The BeamAdapter
plugin for SOFA was used to model these devices for thein
silicoenvironment [26]. This catheter type (straight) does
not have a shaped tip, but it remains possible for an expert
operator to navigate into the right common carotid artery
(RCCA). In contrast, when this catheter type is combined
with the acute angle of the left common carotid artery
(LCCA), an expert operator cannot navigate the testbed – this
allowed us to evaluate a superhuman additional navigation
task (A2L, Figure 1), and evaluate the full capabilities of the
RL agents.
The simulation assumed rigid vessel walls (with an empty
lumen). The simulation’s device behavior was determined
by utilizing a tensile testing machine to measure the tensile
strength of the devices, which facilitated the calculation of
their stiffness [27]. Friction between the wall and device was
iteratively tuned to mimic behavior in a test-bench setup.
This methodology has previously allowed the translation of
autonomous endovascular navigation agents fromin silicoto
in vitroaortic arch models [17].
Inputs (device rotation and translation speed) were applied
at the proximal device end. Rotation and translation speed
were constrained to a maximum of 180 ◦ s−1 and 40mm s−1,
respectively [17]. Similar to a clinical scenario with fluo-
roscopy, feedback during the navigation was given as 2D
(x′, y′)tracking coordinates; no visual information showing
the geometry of the patient vasculature was given.

Ourin vitrotestbed consisted of a 3D-printed transparent
phantom (Clear V4, Formlabs Inc., Somerville, USA), which
utilized a vasculature from thein silicotraining dataset
(Figure 1, Type-I aortic arch). Experiments were conducted
in a mock operating room at St Thomas’ Hospital, London,
UK. Corresponding to clinical MT, fluoroscopic images from
a mobile C-arm (Cios Spin, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen,
Germany) were used as an input to a device tip-tracking
algorithm that extracted the necessary coordinates for the
state-based RL algorithm [28]. Each task was carried out five
times for both types of world model (Section II-E). Agents
were allowed5 minduringin vitroevaluation, to account for
the slower speed of the robotic manipulator (compared toin
silico).
A robotic manipulator (Figure 2) was used to translate and
rotate the catheter and guidewire independently [29].

Model-free SAC and model-based TD-MPC2 algorithms
were used to train the RL agents in this study. The SAC
RL algorithm was implemented from the open-source stEVE
framework [17], which has been shown to be the cur-
rent state-of-the-art for autonomous endovascular interven-
tions [18]. In SAC, the critic learns the value and the
actor optimizes the critic directly to maximize cumulative
rewards [13]. This is useful for continuous action spaces,
leveraging experience replay for data efficiency, but requires
tuning and struggles under high-dimensional inputs [14].
The SAC algorithm used here includes a Long Short-Term
Memory (LSTM) layer for learning trajectory-dependent
state representations and feedforward layers for controlling
the devices [9].

The TD-MPC2 algorithm is designed for sample-
efficient learning and effective planning in continuous action
spaces, combining temporal difference learning with model-
predictive control, while leveraging a learned dynamics
model to simulate environment transitions and plan action
sequences over a short horizon [16]. This approach enables
the agent to optimize actions based on both predicted rewards
and task constraints while using limited real-world interac-
tion. TD-MPC2 incorporates a latent dynamics model and
a cross-entropy planning method, meaning it is particularly

The base TD-MPC2 configuration was used but with an
increased replay buffer size (1×10 7), and an LSTM layer
to function as an observation embedder, allowing storage of
the environment state at each step so that the vessel structure
could be estimated by the path of the device tip.

The RL training process is shown in Figure 3, where
five agents were trained using SAC (one for each defined
phase in Figure 1). Each agent performed 250 navigation
episodes while recording trajectory data (trajectories, actions,
rewards). This data was used to fill the replay buffers before
training the multi-task agents for SAC and TD-MPC2. Each
model was trained for1×10 7 exploration steps, where a
navigation task (or episode) was considered complete when
the target was reached. An episode termination of 200 steps
(≈27 s) was set for computational efficiency. Training was
performed on an NVIDIA DGX A100 node (Santa Clara,
California, USA). Models were trained on 10 patient-specific
vascular anatomies. All models used were trained using the
same vasculatures, parameters, and SAC replay buffer data
as in [10], allowing for validation of this proof-of-concept
study usingin vitroand hold outin silicovasculatures, while
also measuring navigation safety.

The
entire mesh was scaled randomly from0.7−1.3in three
dimensions, and the mesh itself was rotated randomly from
its origin by±30 ◦ in thexandyplane.

A collision monitor on the guidewire tip was implemented
to record the tip contact forcesF x,y,z at each simulation
[10].∥F x,y,z ∥was used to determine the maximum and the
mean tip contact forces recorded duringin silicoevaluation.
To provide robust analysis of the previously proposed train-
ing pipeline [22], the mean/maximum guidewire tip speed
was also recorded duringin silicoevaluation. Additionally,
an ablation study on the effectiveness of the applied data
augmentation techniques was carried out to determine their
effectiveness in translating agents fromin silicotoin vitro.
The ablation study was donein vitrousing the multi-task
SAC agent onA 2R.
During bothin silicoandin vitroevaluation the success
rate (percentage of evaluation episodes where the target is
reached), procedure time (time from the start of navigation
to target point for successful episodes), path ratio (percent-
age distance navigated to target location in unsuccessful
episodes, calculated by dividing guidewire tip total distance
traveled towards target point by the initial distance from
guidewire tip to target point) and exploration steps (number
of training steps taken to reach the point at which the results
are provided) were recorded. Across all experiments and
metrics, reported values were mean±standard deviation,
while comparative statistical analyses were conducted using
two-tailed paired Student’st-tests with a predetermined
significance threshold set atp= 0.05.

evidence_fragments.content:
Results fromin silicoevaluation (Table I) favored TD-
MPC2 over SAC with an increase in mean success rate (58%
to 36% [p <0.001]) and mean path ratio (22% to 49%
[p <0.001]), although taking nearly twice as long (17.1 s to
9.6 s [p <0.001]). Increases in task success rate and path
ratio were seen when moving from a SAC to TD-MPC2
agent:A 2L (SR:8%to38%[p <0.001], PR:21%to40%
[p <0.001]),A 2R (SR:8%to52%[p <0.001], PR:24%to
48%[p <0.001]), andA 3L (SR:16%to38%[p= 0.015],
PR:21%to63%[p <0.001]). An increase in procedure
time was observed acrossA 1 andA 3R when moving from
SAC to TD-MPC2.
An increase in mean and maximum tip force was found
for the TD-MPC2 navigations (mean:p <0.040, max:
p <0.005). No statistically significant difference was found
between the examined models for mean or maximum tip
speed. Exploration steps recorded for SAC and TD-MPC2
were4.5×10 6 (reached after 75 hours) and0.5×10 6 (reached
after 25 hours), respectively.

A significant increase in procedure time
was observed when moving fromin silicotoin vitrofor
both TD-MPC2 (mean timein silico:17.1 s,in vitro:111.0 s
[p <0.001]) and SAC (mean timein silico:9.6 s,in vitro:
66.2 s[p <0.001]). This increase is caused by the delay
between each step (0.5s) necessary for the robot to complete
its movement, and to ensure that the motors did not overheat.

Evaluating the trained models on anin vitrotestbed
showed no difference in mean success rate between TD-
MPC2 and SAC (p= 0.567).

Failure modes using SAC were due to: wrong branch
catheterization (40%,4/10), episode timeout at5mins (30%,
3/10), device leaving the phantom at the origin of the
ascending aorta (20%,2/10), and unable to recover from
device coiling (10%,1/10). The TD-MPC2 failure modes
were: episode timeout (50%,4/8), entering the LCCA during
A2L but not utilizing the catheter effectively to reach the
target further up the branch (25%,2/8), wrong branch
catheterization (13%,1/9), and device leaving the phantom
at the origin of the ascending aorta (13%,1/10).

Thein vitroablation experiment of data augmentation (Ta-
ble III) showed that augmentation provided non-significant
improvement (40%to20%[p= 0.549]).

locator.section_or_table: IV physical transfer and expert experience

evidence_fragments.content:
Both of the trained models were unable to performA 2L
in vitro. Increasing vessel tortuosity and unfavorable carotid
artery take-off angles from the aortic arch can increase
endovascular navigation difficulty [30]. Techniques used to
navigate the LCCAin silicowere not able to be repli-
catedin vitro, potentially due to differences in friction and
device properties. An expert interventional neuroradiologist
(10 years as UK consultant; US attending equivalent) had
experimented on the testbed and confirmed that in a clinical
scenario, specialist catheters would be used, namely a guide
catheter with a slightly bent tip, or a shaped slip catheter such
as a Simmons 2, which has a reverse curve. In summary, in
the current work we have also shown that a singlein silico
trained world model can be effectively transferred to anin
vitrotestbed to complete multiple, non-superhuman (i.e. not
A2L), MT-relevant navigation tasks autonomously.

Additionally, while significant
increases in mean and maximum force were recorded across
tasks for TD-MPC2, all values recorded are well below
a proposed vessel rupture threshold of 1.5N[27].

The
proposed world model leverages existing open-source repos-
itories to maximize reproducibility [17], [16]. TD-MPC2
achieved superior generalization across hold out data com-
pared to SAC, with an increase in success rate and path ratio
in silico. This is the first validation of an autonomous MT
navigation agent in anin vitrotestbed under fluoroscopic
guidance. While improvements in generalization are needed
before clinical deployment, thein vitroresults confirm that
agents trainedin silicocan navigate multiple tasks in physical
models.

capability_assessments.rationale: Implemented learned transitions support an optimizer with simulated control results. Separate L1/L2 predictive-fidelity and L3 comparison experiments are not inherited.
The model-coupled controller performs physical navigation with feedback and reported failures. This is bench control, not patient intervention.
Explicitly model-free comparator; recurrent representation/control do not establish a learned environment transition.

gate_assessments.rationale: Partition/transformations are described, but full provenance, availability, preprocessing and model-selection leakage controls are missing.
Persistent learned transitions are implemented, but successor-prediction evaluation is not reported. L4 does not substitute for G02.
Prediction depth, drift and tolerance-defined usable horizon are not reported. Episode caps are not prediction horizons.
The scoped claim is navigation feasibility, not probabilistic guarantees or uncertainty-dependent decision rules. Uncertainty features remain not_reported.
Command-conditioned planning exists, but timing, calibration, update/support semantics and prediction evaluation are incomplete.
No therapeutic-effect estimand or identified treatment-benefit assurance is evaluated. This does not endorse causal interpretation of device-conditioned predictions.
Decisions and physical mismatch testing exist, but candidate support, complete search settings, reward-exploitation analysis and acceptance criteria are missing.
Simulation bounds provide partial guard evidence; physical guards, abstention, safe stops, injury measurement and justified safety acceptance are unestablished.
Transfer uses one training-anatomy phantom. Independent clinical/site transfer, overlap controls, subgroup behavior and composition acceptance remain insufficiently documented.
Physical execution and quantified discrepancy are evidence, but matching/acceptance criteria do not establish transfer assurance. Informal expert involvement is not a defined human evaluation.
Assessed use is preclinical research, not live patient/workflow utility. Anticipated access/transfer benefits are not realized outcomes.
No defined operational clinical release is reported. Research access gaps remain separate and do not establish authorization.

limitations: Automated model review, not independent human verification or replication.
This synthesis read all seven supplied text pages and earlier image-review notes. Original page images were not directly supplied to this call.
Source path/hash and upstream call receipts are supplied provenance, not newly verified filesystem/API facts. No external cited paper, repository, raw data or supplement was accessed.
Batch-local statements in earlier page notes about unavailable other pages are not global source gaps: their combined coverage spans all seven pages.
All 128 catalogue features receive main-model dispositions. Auxiliary SAC and external-physics scopes are selectively assessed, not claimed separately exhaustive.
Raw evidence preserves extracted table row-merging artifacts. Structured table-cell separation also uses supplied upstream image transcriptions, not direct image reinspection here.
Implemented scope is separately initialized first-phase navigation, not continuous complete thrombectomy, clot retrieval, reperfusion or patient treatment.
CTA-derived anatomical holdouts have simulated navigation outcomes and do not establish held-out actual human clinical transition/outcome validation for R2/R3.
One physical phantom uses a simulation-training anatomy. Phantom control supports R1, not unseen physical-anatomy validation or R6.
An expert's informal testbed experience is human involvement but does not establish a defined model-output evaluation or R4.
Shared lower anatomy, ten training/five held-out upper geometries, predominantly Type-I arches and one phantom restrict generalization and independence.
Rigid empty vessels, incomplete material/friction calibration, unreported tracking errors, coordinate calibration, target tolerance and radiation dose limit safety interpretation.

Transition network, dimension, losses, stochasticity, pretrained parameters, useful history length, candidate count, prediction depth and exact replanning settings remain unreported; cited systems' capabilities are not inherited.
Implemented transitions/evaluated L4 decisions are distinct from unreported standalone predictive fidelity and a separate L3 matched-alternative experiment.
Training budget and earlier result checkpoints are preserved separately. Selection, seeds, pairing, clustering and multiplicity controls remain unclear.
Procedure time conditions on success and path ratio on failure. Algorithms/environments can therefore use different subsets; aggregate weighting and backtracking calculations are unclear.
Episode caps, physical pauses, exploration iterations and prediction horizon are separate. The 0.5 s pause is not inference latency.
Force maxima average episode maxima, not the greatest instantaneous force. The proposed cited 1.5 N reference is not validated here as a tissue/device-specific or universal clinical threshold.
Physical wall-force sensing is future work. Simulated logging, speed bounds and timeouts do not establish comprehensive protection or absence of injury.
Anomalous dispersions, inconsistent failure denominators and prose/table reversals are retained and queued without replacement values.
Nonsignificance is not equivalence; the SAC-only augmentation ablation does not isolate TD-MPC2 dynamics/planning.
Physical mismatch testing does not isolate model exploitation or validate clinical causal effects.
Open-source dependencies and manuscript CC BY do not establish study-specific code, weight, configuration or data release/licenses.
No gate pass, safety guarantee or deployment authorization is asserted.
No files were saved and no executable schema, graph, quotation or semantic validation was run.
